title: Deep Pagination: OFFSET vs Keyset Seek
description: Deep OFFSET pagination re-reads every skipped row; keyset (seek) pagination jumps straight to the next page. Why it matters: pagination is in almost every application with a list view, and OFFSET-based paging is a extremely common pattern that quietly gets worse page by page as users page deeper.
narrative:
## What This Lesson Is About

This lesson is about a pagination technique almost every application uses (page through a list, 20 rows at a time) and a hidden performance cliff that most developers don't discover until their table gets big and users start complaining that "page 500" takes forever to load, even though "page 1" is instant.

The common way developers build pagination is with `OFFSET` and `FETCH NEXT` (or the equivalent in other databases): `ORDER BY OrderId OFFSET 200000 ROWS FETCH NEXT 20 ROWS ONLY` to get, say, page 10,001 of a list sorted by `OrderId`. This reads naturally in English — "skip 200,000 rows, then give me the next 20" — so it feels like it should be cheap, since you're only getting 20 rows back. But it isn't cheap, and the reason is worth really understanding.

Think about how you'd actually find "row 200,001 through 200,020" in a sorted list if you could only move through it in order, like flipping pages in a book rather than teleporting to a bookmark. There's no way to know where "row 200,001" physically sits without first walking past the 200,000 rows before it — the database has to count off every one of those rows to know it's reached the right starting point, even though it then throws all 200,000 of them away and returns only the last 20. `OFFSET` is not a magic jump — it's "read and discard N rows, then read and keep the next M." As the offset grows, so does the wasted work, linearly. Page 2 is nearly free (skip 20, keep 20). Page 10,001 means the database quietly does 200,000+ rows of work just to throw almost all of it away, which is why this lesson's query does roughly 965 logical reads (a "logical read" is one page of data read from the buffer cache or disk — the standard unit SQL Server uses to measure query cost) even though it only returns 20 rows.

The fix is a different pagination strategy called **keyset pagination** (sometimes called "seek pagination" or "the seek method"). Instead of saying "skip N rows," you remember the last row's key value from the *previous* page, and ask a different question entirely: "give me the next 20 rows *after* this specific value." For example, instead of `OFFSET 200000`, you'd write `WHERE OrderId > @lastSeenOrderId ORDER BY OrderId FETCH NEXT 20 ROWS ONLY` (using whatever `OrderId` was on the last row of the page the user just saw). This is a completely different kind of operation from the database's perspective: because the index on `OrderId` is sorted, the engine can directly **seek** to the position right after `@lastSeenOrderId` — jumping straight there, the same way you can flip directly to "page 214" in a book rather than reading every page before it — and then read forward just 20 rows. No matter how deep into the list you are — page 2 or page 10,000 — the cost stays the same: seek to a point, read 20 rows, done. It doesn't get slower as the offset grows, because there is no "offset" anymore — there's only "resume after this specific known point," and the sorted index makes that a fast, direct operation.

There's a practical trade-off worth knowing: keyset pagination doesn't let you jump to an arbitrary page number out of nowhere (like "go directly to page 4,832") the way `OFFSET` technically can — it's built around "next page from here" / "previous page from here" navigation, which is exactly how most real UIs actually work anyway (infinite scroll, "load more," next/previous buttons). If you genuinely need arbitrary random-access page jumps on a huge dataset, that's a harder problem with different trade-offs, but it's rare in practice — most apps only ever page forward sequentially.

Why should you care? Pagination shows up in nearly every application with any kind of list view — order history, search results, activity feeds, admin tables — and `OFFSET`-based pagination is the default pattern in almost every tutorial and ORM example you'll find, which means it's also the default performance trap. It works fine at small scale and then gets progressively, silently worse as the table and the page number both grow, which is exactly the kind of problem that doesn't show up in development or testing (small data, low page numbers) but absolutely shows up in production a few months after launch.

It's worth noticing that this exact problem — cost growing with how deep you page — shows up anywhere a system lets you "skip ahead" through a large ordered list, not just in SQL. Scrolling through very old messages in a chat app, browsing far-back pages of search results, or flipping deep into an old email inbox all have the same underlying tension: if the system has to count through everything before the point you're jumping to, deep jumps get progressively more expensive, no matter how good the underlying storage is. That's exactly why so many modern UIs have shifted away from "page 1, 2, 3... 500" style navigation and toward "load more" / infinite scroll / next-and-previous-only navigation — it's not just a UI preference, it maps naturally onto exactly the kind of pagination (keyset) that stays fast at any depth. If you're designing a new feature from scratch, it's worth choosing "next/previous from a known position" navigation over "jump to page N" navigation specifically because it lets you use the cheaper technique from day one, rather than discovering months later that page 10,000 quietly became the slowest, most complained-about part of the whole application.

One implementation detail worth knowing: keyset pagination requires your ORDER BY column (or columns) to be unique, or at least deterministic as a combination, so that 'resume after this value' always means exactly the same thing. If you're paginating by a non-unique column like OrderDate alone, you'll want to add a unique tiebreaker column (like the primary key) to both the ORDER BY and the WHERE condition, so rows with identical dates don't get skipped or duplicated across pages.

## Scenario
A UI pages through orders 20 at a time. Reaching page 10,001 runs `... ORDER BY OrderId OFFSET 200000 ROWS FETCH NEXT 20 ROWS ONLY`. Returning just 20 rows costs ~965 logical reads and scans the clustered index.

## Why it's slow
`OFFSET` is not a shortcut. SQL Server has no way to teleport to the 200,001st row, so it **reads and discards all 200,000 preceding rows** (a Clustered Index Scan feeding a Top) before emitting your 20. The deeper the page, the more work — page 1 is instant, page 10,001 reads the whole first two-thirds of the table. Cost grows with **offset depth**, which is exactly backwards for a UI where deep pages should be no worse than shallow ones.

## What to look for
- A wide **Clustered Index Scan** under a **Top** operator.
- Reads that scale with the OFFSET value, not with the 20 rows returned.

## The concept
Switch to **keyset (seek) pagination**. Remember the last key from the previous page (`OrderId = 200000`) and ask for `WHERE OrderId > 200000 ORDER BY OrderId` with `TOP (20)`. The clustered index **seeks** directly to that key and reads only the next 20 rows — reads drop from ~965 to a handful, and stay flat no matter how deep the page. The trade-off: keyset needs the last key (not an arbitrary page number), which is a natural fit for infinite-scroll and "next page" APIs.
startingQuery: SELECT OrderId, CustomerId, OrderDate, Total FROM Orders ORDER BY OrderId OFFSET 200000 ROWS FETCH NEXT 20 ROWS ONLY;
hints: OFFSET 200000 doesn't skip cheaply -- SQL Server must read and throw away all 200,000 rows first.
You already know the last key of the previous page (OrderId 200000). Seek past it instead of counting to it.
Use WHERE OrderId > 200000 ORDER BY OrderId with TOP (20) so the clustered index seeks straight to the page.
